newsitem.title: USA: Trex sees mammography sales boom on horizon.
newsitem.headline: Trex sees mammography sales boom on horizon.

text.p: Trex Medical Corp said Tuesday it is poised to take advantage of a likely explosion in sales of full-breast digital mammography equipment when the new technology is approved by federal regulators.

Trex, the world's leading supplier of mammography equipment and stereotactic biopsy systems for the detection of breast cancer, hopes to have a digital machine on the market in 1998, president and chief executive Hal Kirshner told Reuters.

Kirshner said in an interview he could not predict how long it would take to win approval by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. "But we're hopeful that we will file and get approval so that we can be on the market in 1998."

He said the FDA has been "extremely cooperative" and speedy in granting product approvals for Trex in the past. Trex is a subsidiary of ThermoTrex Corp, which in turn is a unit of ThermoElectron Co of Waltham, Mass.
Kirshner said that Trex's Danbury-based Lorad Division was doubling its space to 123,000 square feet, including a quadrupling of its manufacturing space.
He declined to give an investment figure.
Trex's Lorad Division united last year with three other medical imaging companies to form Trex Medical Corp.
In addition to Lorad, Trex is made up of Bennett X-Ray Technologies of Copiague, N.Y.; XRE Corp of Littleton, Mass.; and Continental X-Ray Corp of Broadview, Ill.
Kirshner said Trex posted year-on-year sales growth of 67 percent to $55 million during the first quarter of fiscal year 1997.
"Though we're experiencing sales growth because of acquisitions, I want to point out that we are still growing internally at Lorad," he said.
Lorad's sales grew to $100 million in 1996, from just $13 million in 1990, he said.
Lorad now has 360 employees, compared to 100 in 1990. Trex Medical has about 1,200 employees around the world.
"There's been dramatic growth at Lorad, which prompted the acquisition of Bennett and expanded Lorad's market presence into general X-ray and other areas," Kirshner said.
"We broadened the x-ray base and expanded into much larger markets where our strong technology, which is digital detection, can then be applied to all other x-rays."

Kirshner estimated that the worldwide market for mammography and stereotactic biopsy equipment was now worth up to $500 million in annual sales. He said Trex was the industry leader in both areas, but declined to give market share.
He said sales of stereotactic biopsy equipment would surge as the technology caught on. Digital technology has received clearance thus far only for stereotactic needle biopsies, not for screenings.
"We've just really scratched the surface. I think we've got about 1,000 (stereotactic) units installed worldwide on prone biopsy tables, versus a potential of about 10,000."
The potential market for digital mammography machines was much larger than for conventional film-screen devices, he said.
The eventual approval of the technology will fuel a demand for replacement machines, he said.
He said that over the next 10-12 years, some 13,000 digital units would be sold in the U.S., and another 10,000 overseas.
"So if you're looking at 20,000 units times an average price of $300,000, you're talking about a $6-billion market over the next 10 years," he said.
Kirshner said the current debate over early detection of breast cancer was helping raise product awareness.
In a controversial decision, an expert panel of the National Institutes of Health decided last month not to recommend regular mammograms for women in their forties.
But many physicians found the decision shocking, since it seemed to ignore conventional wisdom that early detection of breast tumors could save lives.

"Any debate on mammography is going to create more awareness of the value of mammograms," Kirshner said. "I think all of the discussions agree that mammography is still the best modality for early detection of breast cancer. The question is whether it makes sense for women under 50 to go."
--Matthew Lewis, Hartford newsroom (860) 727-0224
